Q: Python multiprocessing works in script but hangs in Windows Server A:

On all Windows systems (Windows 10 / Windows Server 2019), Python’s multiprocessing.Pool uses the spawn start method by default, which has strict requirements:

Q: R DropBox access example without rdrop2 A:

The first three steps need to be done just once.

Step1. Create a DropBox app. This requires going to https://www.dropbox.com/developers , selecting the "App Console" tab, then selecting the "Create App" button and following the various menus. On the DropBox page for the created app there will be an "App key" and an "App secret". Write these down on a piece of paper for later use.

Step 2. Get a temporary (10 minute) authorisation code from DropBox by going to this website (after swapping <APP_KEY> for the app key discovered in step 1) : https://www.dropbox.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=\<APP_KEY>&token_access_type=offline&response_type=code

The web site will ask you for permission to grant access to your DropBox app and then eventually give you a longish character string. This is your authorisation code. Add it to your piece of paper.

Step 3. Get a permanent refresh code using the following r code. Add it to your piece of paper.

#Get app_key and app_secret from DropBox.com/developers
app_key    <- "stringOfCharacters" 
app_secret <- "differentStringOfCharacters"

#Get the authorisation code from https://www.dropbox.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=<APP_KEY>&token_access_type=offline&response_type=code
authorization_code <- "anotherStringOfCharacters" 

# Request a permanent refresh token
RefreshTokenResponse <- httr::POST(
  url = "https://api.dropbox.com/oauth2/token",
  body = list(
    code = authorization_code,
    grant_type = "authorization_code",
    client_secret = app_secret,
    client_id = app_key
  ),
  encode="form"
)

Refresh_token <- httr::content(RefreshTokenResponse)$refresh_token

Step 4. Get a temporary (3 hour) access code. This needs to be done prior to every time you want to use the DropBox API.

AccessTokenResponse <- httr::POST(
  url = "https://api.dropbox.com/oauth2/token",
  body = list(
    refresh_token = Refresh_token,
    grant_type = "refresh_token",
    client_secret = app_secret,
    client_id = app_key
  ),
  encode="form"
)

Access_token <- httr::content(AccessTokenResponse)$access_token

Step 5. Use the access token in your call to the DropBox API. For example, to list the contents of a directory:

DropBoxPathToList <- "/Directory/SubDirectory"
DropBoxList <- httr::POST(
  url = "https://api.dropboxapi.com/2/files/list_folder",
  add_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer",Access_token)),
  content_type_json(),
  body = toJSON(list(path = DropBoxPathToList),auto_unbox = TRUE))
DropBoxListData <- fromJSON(httr::content(DropBoxList, type ="text",encoding="UTF-8"),flatten = TRUE)
DropBoxFiles <- DropBoxListData$entries

Q: How to use better OOP for a Huffman Compressor A:

It's a personal project I'm doing. I'm trying to build a data compression pipeline that reads a .txt file, builds a frequency table, makes an encoding table, and encodes a compressed file with the encoding table and can also decompress it. Then, I plan on doing performance optimizations to improve throughput (faster frequency counting, reading the bytes from the file directly, doing stuff in parallel, etc.) My goal with using OOP is really just to make better project structure so that it becomes much easier to use modularity to identify what parts of the program need optimization, along with designing a more encapsulated pipeline where users only have to worry about compression and decompression.

Q: Command 'python' not found after creating conda environment A:

Sorry for all the fuss but I have solved the problem. Since Ubuntu 19.10 doesn't come with python2 pre-installed what I did to get rid of the problem was to first remove python (since I installed it after installing conda, note that this is python and not python3 since python3 comes pre-installed) and conda completely with the following lines.

sudo apt-get purge --auto-remove python

rm -rf ~/miniconda3

rm -rf ~/.condarc ~/.conda ~/.continuum

After this I installed python

sudo apt install python

And after installing python I installed conda the normal way and now I don't get any of the error messages posted when I open up a terminal. I guess order of PATH variables matters. Since when I had troubles I first installed conda and followed up by installing python and think that condas python path might have come first.
